annotations.text:
Four directions for the same moment: hand #23, flop 9h 7s 2c, Chip has bet $40, it's your turn on the button with As Kd.

Same data everywhere, so the only thing that varies is the design. All four already fold in the game-loop fixes: street stepper, split pot ($115 committed + $80 still in play), position labels, speed control, session P&L, keyboard hints, and a persistent action bar.

Pick one, or mix — 'B's feed with A's table' is a perfectly good answer.

A · BROADCAST — you're sitting at the table.
Cinematic felt oval, warm bronze rail, action shown as bubbles that pop above the acting seat and fade. Hero's cards live big in the bottom rail, not in a seat.

Best at: making a hand feel like an event. Familiar to anyone who has played online poker.
Costs: history is ephemeral — you see the last action, not the last ten. Least useful of the four when you want to study a hand. Heaviest to build.

B · STUDIO — poker as an instrument panel.
Flat table on the left, permanent right rail on the right: full hand feed grouped by street, live pot-odds readout, recent-hand results. Seat plates are data tiles in tabular mono.

Best at: you can always reconstruct why the pot is what it is. The rail is also where a future 'reads / tells' panel would go, so it's the direction that grows into the psychology layer.
Costs: colder, less table-feel. The rail has to become a bottom sheet on iPhone.

C · EDITORIAL — the flat/minimal spec in your plan, taken literally.
Warm paper, ink hairlines, Newsreader serif for every number, one vermillion accent. No felt, no gradients, no glow. Actions read as prose: 'bets $40', 'folds'.

Best at: legibility, calm, and the smallest visual-debt bill. Inverts to a dark theme cleanly by swapping tokens.
Costs: it doesn't feel like gambling. If you want the pulse of a real table, this isn't it.

D · FOCUS — decision-first, phone-native.
Drops the round table entirely. Opponents compress into a strip of tiles, board and your cards get the space instead. One column, no eye travel, 62px hit targets.

Best at: iPhone. It's the only direction where the phone layout is the design rather than a squeeze of the desktop one. Fastest to read under pressure.
Costs: no table metaphor means less social presence — six tiles feel less like six opponents. Scales awkwardly past ~8 players.

iPhone portrait, 390 × 844.

No status bar or home indicator drawn — the real ones sit on top, so that space is left clear.

Worth judging here specifically: can you read your own two cards at a glance, and can you hit the action buttons with a thumb without looking? A and D pass easily; B trades card size for the feed; C is the most readable but the least tappable.
